extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and students interested in UK media, press ethics, and political scandals
extracted.subtask_short: wikipedia article on phone hacking scandal
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of the News International / News of the World phone hacking scandal: history, investigations, legal actions, inquiries (Leveson), and public/political fallout in the UK. Covers investigative operations, regulatory responses, arrests, settlements and wider ethical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Complaints Commission guidance on use of subterfuge/public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCC's 2007 inquiry concluded: "there is a legitimate place for the use of subterfuge when there are grounds in the public interest to use it and it is not possible to obtain information through other means".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a journalistic-standard criterion: subterfuge (e.g., covert information-gathering) may be acceptable only when there are clear public-interest grounds and no alternative means to obtain the information. The article records that the PCC applied this test in reviewing News of the World's conduct and that debates about the scope of 'public interest' were central to inquiries and criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlawful interception offence (Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000, section 79)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accessing voicemail by hacking was treated as an offence under section 79 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard: persons who unlawfully intercepted voicemail could be arrested and prosecuted under RIPA (the article cites arrests and convictions — e.g., Clive Goodman and Glenn Mulcaire pleaded guilty and received custodial sentences). This criterion distinguishes lawful newsgathering from criminal conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of privacy as civil claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims brought civil claims for breach of privacy against News International; settlements and apologies were used to resolve many cases (the article cites multiple payouts and settlements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil-justice standard: proof of unlawful intrusion into private communications or misuse of private information can ground damages and settlement. The article gives examples (e.g., Sienna Miller, Gordon Taylor, Max Clifford) showing how privacy-law outcomes influenced public and corporate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Commissioner's Office findings on illegal acquisition of personal information
rubrics_metrics.description: Operation Motorman (ICO) uncovered large-scale purchase and use of confidential personal information from unregistered computer databases and other improper sources; ICO reports include 'What price privacy?' and 'What price privacy now?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory/data-protection standard: media organizations should not obtain or use personal data from unlawful or unregistered sources; invoices and transaction records identified journalists and publications buying personal information, prompting ICO reports and criticism. The ICO evidence was used to evaluate the scale and illegality of information-gathering practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry remit / Leveson Inquiry terms of reference (press ethics and policing of the press)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Leveson Inquiry was established to "look into phone hacking and police bribery by the News of the World and consider the wider culture and ethics of the British newspaper industry," and to examine effective regulation (the article notes that the PCC would be replaced 'entirely').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative framework, the Inquiry's remit sets standards for assessing press conduct, institutional responsibility, and regulatory adequacy — i.e., whether newspapers, regulators and police met ethical and legal obligations, and what structural reforms were needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution/evidentiary thresholds as applied by Crown Prosecution Service and police
rubrics_metrics.description: The article describes disputes over whether there was 'sufficient grounds or evidence' for further arrests and prosecutions, noting that Assistant Commissioner John Yates reported insufficient fresh material while committees criticized the police for not pursuing evidence; it also notes that the CPS provided criteria used by police to limit scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative/prosecutorial standard: CPS evidentiary guidelines and the police's interpretation of them determined whether alleged misconduct was pursued criminally. The piece highlights how decisions about evidentiary thresholds and prosecutorial advice shaped the scale of investigations and resultant accountability.
